title: Classroom Layout
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: This DistillED newsletter edition makes the case that classroom layout -- seating, walls, sightlines, light -- is an evidence-backed lever on behaviour and learning, not an aesthetic afterthought. It walks through the research base: the HEAD project's finding that physical design explains 16% of variance in learning progress, Wheldall and Lam's classic finding that rows roughly double on-task behaviour compared to table groups, and Fisher, Godwin and Seltman's study showing heavily decorated walls nearly halve learning gains. It also draws on proximity research showing that sitting near an attentive, hard-working peer measurably lifts a student's own effort and attention, independent of whether they can see that peer. The piece translates all of this into five practical, budget-free setup decisions teachers can make before students arrive: choosing a default arrangement by task, building an assigned A/B seating plan, placing students deliberately rather than alphabetically, ensuring sightlines and circulation to every seat, and clearing a wall while protecting natural light. The overall argument is that the room either protects a teacher's instruction or silently taxes it, and that most of the highest-impact changes cost nothing beyond deliberate planning.
points: Classroom design is not decorative: the HEAD project found physical layout choices account for roughly 16% of the variance in pupils' learning progress.
Teacher-assigned seating sharply cuts disruption compared with student-chosen seating, with the effect strongest during individual work.
Wall displays follow a non-linear curve -- both bare and heavily-decorated walls reduce on-task behaviour, with roughly 20-30% wall coverage predicting the best attention.
Proximity is a lever on effort, not just behaviour: students paired with an attentive, hard-working peer work and attend harder themselves, even on unrelated tasks.
The piece translates the research into five concrete setup steps -- task-based default arrangement, A/B seating plans, deliberate placement, sightlines/circulation, and a cleared, light-filled wall.
quotes: Research from the HEAD project found that classroom design accounted for 16% of the variation in pupils' learning progress

Disruptive behavior during group seating occurred at twice the rate when students chose their seats than when the teacher chose. During individual seating, disruptive behavior occurred more than three times as often when the students chose their seats.

Fisher, Godwin and Seltman (2014) taught the same science lessons to kindergarteners in rooms with heavily decorated walls and in sparse ones. In the decorated room, students were off-task 39% of the time versus 28% in the sparse room and their learning gains nearly halved, from 33% down to 18%.
Desender and Van den Bussche (2015) found that students paired with a partner exerting more effort on a task increased their own effort too, even on a completely different task.
None of this means the room does the teaching for you. It means the room either protects the attention your teaching depends on, or it quietly taxes it before you've started.
Letting students choose their own seats roughly doubles disruption in group seating and triples it in individual seating, compared with a teacher-assigned plan.
